L51: Several Chinese owners of Tesla’s new cite35†Model Y L , the larger 3-row version of the popular Model Y, are going to Chinese social media to complain about suspension collapse issues – and it’s enough of a problem that fans have developed a “finger method” to test whether a vehicle is affected.
L52: Tesla released the Model Y L in China cite39†almost exactly one year ago , and the model got cite40†okay reviews in the brutally competitive Chinese Ev market. It had several improvements over the standard Model Y at the time, and a larger wheel base which allowed for a third row of seats – though those rear seats could only be occupied by rather small people.
L53: The model did debut to an impressive wave of sales, but over the longer term, Tesla sales in China have cite41†continued to fall – though perhaps less than the sales of other foreign brands that are getting absolutely crushed by domestic electric vehicle competition.
L54: 
L55: Now, Tesla seems to be seeing a new set of problems, at least according to Chinese social media reports.
L56: The issue was recently covered on cite42†Sina.com†k.sina.com.cn and cite43†CarNewsChina†carnewschina.com , but the first collection of reports seems to have been posted in early August on cite44†smzdm.com†post.smzdm.com , a Chinese product review/recommendation site (the name seems to be Chinese shorthand for “What’s Worth Buying”).
L57: The report says that in the period of June through August, Chinese social media had seen a pattern of complaints of rear suspension collapse on the new longer, heavier vehicles. The complaints were sourced from Xiaohongshu, sometimes referred to in the West as “Chinese Instagram.”
L58: 
L59: Users posted various photos of Model Y L vehicles with low rear wheel arches, with smzdm finding at least ten posts showing the same issue, and hundreds of comments on those posts complaining.
L60: On those posts, owners have developed a “finger test” for other owners to follow as a simple check whether their vehicle might be affected. Simply put your hand inbetween the wheel and wheel arch: if 4 fingers fit, you’re fine; if 3 fingers fit, watch out; if fewer than 3 fingers fit, your suspension has probably been affected by this issue.
L61: 
L62: cite45†Image cite46†Image L63: A more accurate test can be done with a measuring tape, measuring from the ground. Normal heights run from 764-804mm. If your wheel arch is less than 764mm off the ground, this will qualify for a replacement from Tesla, per its service guidelines.
L64: 
L65: A lower rear suspension can dangerously affect handling characteristics, and at the very least alters tire wear patterns to prematurely wear out tires. Some users report a feeling of “swaying” at the rear of affected vehicles.
L66: Most of the affected vehicles seem to have come from the first batch of cars, delivered in September and October of 2025. These cars have mostly been fixed under warranty, but the issue has recurred for some of the vehicles even after service was done on them.
L67: But users are suggesting vigilance. Since Tesla China has not yet made a statement about the issue, social media users have suggested that owners should check their suspension monthly, and keep a log of the heights – either measured with a tape or with fingers, and taking photos to keep track of it all.
L68: This is particularly true for older vehicles from the early batches. It could be that Tesla has improved its processes since then, or it could be that the issue just hasn’t become apparent yet on newer vehicles.
L69: 
L70: So far, it seems that most vehicles are having the issue solved under warranty, but vigilance is still important. The same applies to overseas Y L owners with Shanghai-assembled cars, such as those in Australia and New Zealand, who should keep an eye on their rear suspension.
L71: This isn’t the first time Tesla has had suspension issues. The US NHTSA is currently cite47†probing Tesla over suspension failure (which cite48†it has done before ), though those are about the front suspension, not the rear. And in Germany, the Model Y was found to have a cite49†high defect rate in annual testing, with suspension being the main source of issues.
L72: Whether this same rear suspension issue will affect the US version of the Model Y L, which was just cite50†launched in July , is another question. Chinese models are assembled in Tesla’s Shanghai factory, and US models are assembled in Texas. There have been differences between US and Shanghai-built models in the past, so we really have no idea yet whether this problem will be present on US models. Until Tesla develops and announces a fix, keep your fingers ready.

L51: Tesla said today that its Robotaxis have driven a total of 1 million miles without a human driver supervising them. The number is more than double what we heard at the last check-in just six weeks ago, as Tesla finally shifts away from human “safety drivers.”
L52: Tesla cite39†launched its Robotaxi service in Austin last June, and it got off to an cite40†interesting start. The system made several goofs, only had a few cars available, and cars were monitored by a “safety driver” sitting in the front seat with access to some vehicle controls if anything looked like it was going wrong.
L53: Since then, the system has improved and added cite41†more cities , and Tesla has cite42†mostly removed drivers (it first cite43†put them in a chase car , now it just cite44†allows occasional remote control of the vehicles).
L54: 
L55: Now, there are actually Robotaxis driving around in “unsupervised” mode – that is, the car and its on-board software is doing all the sensing and control the vehicle needs, instead of being driven by a human anywhere in the chain of command.
L56: The last time we heard from Tesla, during its Q2 earnings call on July 22, Tesla had done 380,000 total miles of unsupervised driving with what it said were “zero notable incidents” (at least 17 of which were, uh, cite45†noted in government documents , as of May). This sounds like a big number of miles, but that’s not even the number of miles one average American will drive in their lifetime, so it’s not exactly a huge sample size.
L57: But that sample is getting larger, and indeed getting larger somewhat quickly.
L58: 
L59: Despite Tesla taking more than a year worth of Robotaxi operation to get to 380,000 unsupervised miles, it has now put up another 620,000 miles in just the last 6 weeks, according to Tesla VP of Autopilot/AI Ashok Elluswamy.
L60: 
L61: Elluswamy made the announcement at Tesla’s Cybercab event earlier today, stating “I’m happy to announce that we have achieved 1 million miles of unsupervised Robotaxi operation.”
L62: Note the use of the word “unsupervised” here. This is not the weasel word that Tesla uses to refer to, for example, its cite42†human-driven ride-hailing service in the Bay Area , which it claims to be a Robotaxi but is really just Tesla employees driving Model Ys with FSD turned on some of the time. Tesla uses the word “unsupervised” to refer to truly autonomous miles, without a human involved.
L63: The sudden addition of 620,000 unsupervised miles in just a few weeks may make it seem that the Tesla Robotaxi network is accelerating rapidly, but let’s not get too hasty. Prior to a few months ago, all of Tesla’s Robotaxi miles were supervised by a human, it was only at the beginning of this year that Tesla started doing any unsupervised miles at all. Now, basically all of its (non-Bay-Area) miles are done unsupervised.
L64: And Tesla claimed that Robotaxi miles were growing rapidly, but last we checked in during the Q2 earnings call, paid ridership was cite46†flat, not growing , at around 900k added miles in each of the last two quarters. As of that update, Tesla had put up around two and a half million paid miles, 380,000 of which were unsupervised.
L65: With this new update showing at least 620,000 more miles added in the last 6 weeks – nevermind the other half of the quarter not accounted for in that number, and any additional paid but not unsupervised miles from the human Bay Area service – it looks like Tesla will probably increase its total paid Robotaxi miles this quarter again. So the service should be back to growth, instead of stalling as it had last quarter.

L50: Weeks after a Tesla Model 3 sat stopped in a live Florida interstate lane and its driver was killed, it happened again — a 2020 Model 3, stopped dead on a Phoenix-area freeway at 3 a.m., rear-ended by a pickup, its driver dead at the scene.
L51: And as in the cite38†Florida case that we revealed today, no one investigating knew what Tesla’s own data shows: the car’s driver-assist system was engaged.
L52: 
L53: This article is part of an ongoing Electrek investigation that uncovers fatal crashes involving Tesla’s ADAS system that the automaker is trying to hide through redactions in its NHTSA reports. You can keep track of the investigation through cite39†this hub .
L54: ## What happened on Loop 202
L55: 
L56: Just after 3 a.m. on October 31, 2025, a Tesla sedan was struck from behind by a Ford F-350 pickup on the eastbound Loop 202 (Red Mountain) freeway near Dobson Road in Mesa, Arizona. The Tesla’s driver died at the scene, and the eastbound freeway was closed for hours, cite40†Arizona’s Family (KPHO/KTVK) and 12News reported†www.azfamily.com .
L57: The initial coverage was thin — the Arizona Department of Public Safety said only that two vehicles were involved and didn’t detail injuries. No report identified the car as a Tesla with a driver-assist system, and none mentioned Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving.”
L58: ## What Tesla told the federal government
L59: 
L60: Electrek matched that crash to a redacted report in Tesla’s filings to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, under a Standing General Order that requires automakers to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact.
L61: In the report, Tesla identifies the vehicle as a 2020 Model 3, marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” and lists the car’s pre-crash movement as “Stopped” at 0 mph in a freeway lane, in clear weather with no unusual road conditions. It says the Tesla was struck across its entire rear by the front of the pickup — a straightforward rear-end into a stationary car.
L62: Crucially, Tesla says it holds the event-data recorder, telematics, and video from the car — everything needed to show why it was stopped. Then it redacts the three fields that would explain it: the crash narrative, the software version (which hides whether it was Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving”), and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area — all as “confidential business information,” the cite41†same redactions Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports .
L63: We’ve compiled the full NHTSA record for this crash, showing exactly what Tesla disclosed and what it blacked out.
L64: 
L65: cite42†Image L66: ## A pattern, not a one-off
L67: 
L68: This is now the second fatal crash Electrek has documented with the same signature: a 2020 Tesla Model 3, driver-assist verified engaged, stopped at 0 mph in a live freeway lane, rear-ended, its driver killed — both in October 2025, one in Florida and one in Arizona.
L69: There is an obvious candidate for why a driver-assist car would stop in traffic. Tesla has a long-documented cite43†phantom braking problem , in which Autopilot brakes hard for obstacles that aren’t there — an issue that drew an NHTSA investigation and a class-action suit. A system that stopped the car in a travel lane, or failed to keep it moving, would fit. So would a driver medical event with the system holding the car. Only Tesla’s data distinguishes between them. Both are problematic.
L70: How we know it’s the same crash: NHTSA leaves a few fields unredacted — city, vehicle, month, and an incident time logged in UTC. Converted to Arizona time, Tesla’s timestamp lands at about 3 a.m. on the same freeway, with the same fatal outcome and the same 2020 Model 3 that DPS and local outlets reported.
L71: Electrek has filed a public-records request with the Arizona Department of Public Safety for the crash report, and to ask whether Tesla shared its data — the raw telematics, or only its own interpretation of it — with investigators.
L72: Electrek has contacted DPS to let them know Tesla confirmed its ADAS was active at the time of the crash and to ask whether Tesla communicated that to the authorities.
L73: ## Electrek’s Take
L74: 
L75: As always, we don’t know that Tesla’s driver-assist caused this death, any more than we do in the Florida case. But two men are dead in nearly identical circumstances a few weeks apart, both in cars that Tesla’s own records say had the driver-assist engaged and stopped in a live freeway lane — and in both, Tesla is holding the data that would explain it while the investigating agency is left without.

L66: The driver was Steven Alvarez, 23, an IT technician at Lake Jackson Intermediate School and a Brazoswood High School graduate, according to Brazosport ISD, which mourned him publicly. Local outlets reported that on the afternoon of May 20, 2026, his car left Brazoswood Drive, crashed through a fence at Clute Municipal Park, and hit the complex of a decommissioned, empty pool, where it caught fire.
L67: Clute police said their preliminary belief was that Alvarez had suffered a medical episode. No outlet mentioned Autopilot, “Full Self-Driving,” or any Tesla driver-assist system. The 104 mph figure exists only in Tesla’s telematics.
L68: ## What could have happened — and why we can’t tell
L69: 
L70: Tesla’s data confirms one thing: the driver-assist system was on. It does not, on its own, tell us what role the system played. Several possibilities are consistent with the redacted record.
L71: 
L72: The system could have been actively driving in a way that contributed to the crash. But Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” do not normally take a car to 104 mph on a residential street on their own, which points toward driver input.
L73: Tesla’s speed figure could be wrong. SGO speed fields are self-reported and occasionally inconsistent, and 104 mph is extreme for the setting. It deserves independent verification against the police crash report and any physical evidence.
L74: Or the police theory and Tesla’s data could both be right at once: Alvarez may have suffered a medical emergency and involuntarily pressed the accelerator while the system was engaged, pushing the car past any speed the software would command. That is close to what Tesla says happened in the cite40†fatal Katy, Texas crash , where it admits “Full Self-Driving” was on but blames the driver for flooring the accelerator to 73 mph.
L75: The point is that the public cannot distinguish between these scenarios — and neither can investigators working only from the public file — because Tesla sealed the narrative, the software version, and the operating-area field.
L76: ## Electrek’s Take

L78: I want to be careful here, because a young man died and his family deserves accuracy, not a narrative. We do not know that Tesla’s driver-assist caused this crash. It’s entirely possible a medical emergency did, with the system a bystander.

L53: Tesla has a packed September ahead of it, with two confirmed and one rumored product launches. For a company that has gone so long without new products, it would be a big month… if all three of those products hadn’t been launched years ago already.
L54: 
L55: It’s September 2026, and we’ve got a lot to look forward to in the EV space.
L56: First up, we’re finally going to see the cite41†launch of the Tesla Cybercab this Thursday, September 3. The Cybercab is a small, two-seat vehicle intended to be used fully autonomously as a robotaxi, and doesn’t even have a steering wheel or pedals, as it’s meant to operate without a driver at all times.
L57: Second, Tesla has confirmed that late this month it will cite42†roll out the Tesla Semi , a fully-electric heavy duty semi truck. This promises to make goods delivery more efficient, which is important given that larger vehicles are responsible for cite43†well more than their fair share†www.ucs.org of the pollution that harms human health. There are other electric semis, but Tesla claims to offer a cite44†better value proposition than the rest of them.
L58: Finally, there’s the specter of the next-gen Tesla Roadster. While nothing is announced yet, Tesla designer Franz von Holzhausen cite45†said the Roadster is coming “very soon,” and we have heard some rumors suggesting the month of September. The Tesla Roadster is meant to be a fully electric hypercar with bonkers performance specs, which CEO Elon Musk has said will be cite46†the “last best driver’s car” but also says that it will be able to “fly” (which cite47†doesn’t make sense ).
L59: It would be an exciting month… if we hadn’t been hearing about all of these products for years now.
L60: ## Cybercab unveiled in 2024, but the idea is much older
L61: 
L62: The Cybercab is the newest of the three, having been cite48†originally revealed in 2024 . That’s an acceptable time between reveal and production, if actually even a little quick (well, as long as we’re not cite49†comparing to China’s EV timelines ).
L63: But that ignores the years of robotaxi-related talk from Musk, who originally cite50†suggested way back in 2016 that Tesla owners who purchased FSD (software which the company sold for cite51†as much as $15,000 and cite52†still has not delivered ) would be able to send their cars out as autonomous taxis to make them money.
L64: At the time, this was meant to apply to Tesla’s consumer vehicles, and Tesla called the concept “cite53†Tesla Network .” Now, it’s branding it as “Robotaxi,” and Tesla has sent out its own vehicles to make money using FSD, cite53†but still won’t let you do it , despite that it sold software on the promise that you could (and that this software would turn cars into an “cite54†appreciating asset ” due to gradual technological unlocks).
L65: Tesla even cite55†cancelled the planned Model 2 , an affordable consumer vehicle, to make room for the stripped-down Cybercab, which we have no indication will be purchaseable by consumers.
L66: And don’t forget: Tesla has not solved self-driving. Neither the consumer-available FSD nor the Robotaxi-exclusive version that allows operation without someone in the driver’s seat is truly capable of unattended operation at all times, or even in more than a few geofenced areas. Releasing a car with no steering wheel cite56†makes no sense before you solve that problem.
L67: So while we’ll soon see the Cybercab in cite57†some sort of action , it is based on a concept that is more than a decade late, it still doesn’t deliver on its promises, and Tesla turned it from something that would be publicly-available and that people spent tens of thousands of dollars on into something that Tesla alone can operate and potentially profit on, while consumers are restricted from doing the thing they were promised when they bought their product.
L68: ## Tesla Semi was first shown in 2017, almost a decade ago
L69: 
L70: The Tesla Semi does stand to revolutionize trucking – or at least, it did 9 years ago when it was first shown with a planned 2020 release.
L71: 
L72: Electrek cite58†attended that event , and heard the pronouncements about how the Semi would take over trucking. It would beat diesel trucks in all-in cost per mile, so there’s really no reason a fleet manager should bother buying a diesel truck ever again.
L73: Except, of course, that the Semi has not been available. Despite a whole bleacher full of fleet managers being invited to that event for dealmaking purposes, the Semi took its sweet time to get to scale.
L74: Tesla did cite59†deliver its first Semis in late 2022, late but not so late, and that first batch went to PepsiCo and its subsidiary Frito-Lay. And then… not much happened. We didn’t get official counts, but by looking through cite60†recall paperwork, it was clear that Semis were being assembled at a cite61†glacial pace , if at all.
L75: Since 2021, Tesla has also said that a cite62†dedicated Semi production line was being worked on at its Nevada battery factory. Over the years there has been cite63†progress on that line , but it has been quite slow.
L76: 
L77: Finally, this year, cite64†the first truck rolled off the dedicated high-volume line , and Semis have been trickling out to cite65†other cite66†customers over time (and cite67†we finally got to ride in one at ACT Expo last year).
L78: So Tesla’s new event to cite42†“rollout” the Semi is a little confusing, given that the truck was already cite58†unveiled at an event in 2017, cite59†delivered at an event in 2022, and the factory cite64†started working in April 2026 . We’re not really sure what the purpose is for this event, although the next product might give us more of a hint…
L79: ## The Roadster might get launched, or might get pushed back… for stock pumping reasons
L80: 
L81: The Roadster is another continually delayed product. First unveiled in the cite58†same event as the Tesla Semi in 2017, it was promised to be the car that gave a “cite68†hard-core smack down to gasoline powered cars.” But now in 2026, we still don’t have a definitive idea of when it will be released.
L82: Now, perhaps you’ll say that the Roadster doesn’t fit in this article, since there’s no announced launch in September like the other two products. But there was cite69†supposed to be a demo in August , which ended yesterday, and a demo has been cite70†announced and cite71†pushed back many times prior.
L83: 
L84: (But even if we do skip the Roadster, we could throw in cite72†FSD being able to avoid potholes as a planned product upgrade, which was first announced in 2019, and which cite72†Musk said this week is “coming soon” )
L85: But more importantly, another recent statement from a former Tesla president could shine some light on the real reason for all these events: that the Roadster delays have all been about cite73†bringing Tesla and SpaceX closer together .
L86: The connection is particularly clear in the case of the Roadster, which Musk said early on would be available with a “cite74†SpaceX package ” to increase performance further, which Musk said would be cite75†demonstrated by “the end of next year” in 2019 (hmm, where have I cite76†heard that phrase before†en.wikipedia.org …).
L87: Originally, that SpaceX package was marketed as using cold gas thrusters to help performance. This is theoretically possible and could be beneficial, if they were used for lateral thrust or additional downforce and if weight was kept down.
L88: But later Musk started saying nonsense like the car would be able to “cite75†hover ” or “cite77†fly “, which does not actually provide a performance benefit (nobody is ever looking for “upforce”). We’ve found cite47†other performance patents that would actually be kind of cool, but all the rhetoric has been about SpaceX, flying, rockets and so on.
L89: 
L90: So why talk about all this stuff if it doesn’t help performance? Well, maybe it’s about a different kind of performance: stock performance.
